extracted.intended_audience: experimental scientists (physicists and physiologists), Royal Society readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting methodological and quality criteria for designing, conducting, and judging physical and physiological experiments (instrumentation, controls, timing, and interpretation) as illustrated by 19th‑century Royal Society papers on barometry, digestion, and friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument sensibility (assignable degree of sensibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the principle on which it is constructed is such, that any assignable degree of sensibility may be given to it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruments so their sensitivity can be tuned (here by choice and mixture of fluids: oil, water, alcohol, ether). Example: mixing alcohol with water to reduce specific gravity difference increases scale of variations; using olive oil gives about eleven times the variation compared with water alone. Note limits: certain fluids (ether) reach practical limits of sensibility or inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness and practical convenience of instrumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for instruments that are 'very compact in its form' as opposed to unwieldy long columns (e.g., columns of water would be 'exceedingly incommodious').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance sensitivity against practicality — avoid designs that are too large to use even if they offer greater raw sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and adjustment before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument is 'adjusted ready for use' when 'the two surfaces of the water in the two legs are seen to be on the same level, or have been rendered so, by equalizing the pressures of the incumbent columns of oil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish and document a clear calibration/state-of‑zero procedure (e.g., equal levels) before measurement and ensure repeatable setup steps (equal measures of oil, specified fluid depths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement principle and correct interpretation of observable change
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize what physical difference actually measures the applied quantity: 'it is not, however, the entire excess of the longer column of water which in this case acts as an equipoise... the pressure exerted is only the difference between the column of water and an equal column of oil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully derive how observed instrument displacement maps to the true measured variable; account for counteracting effects (e.g., elongation of oil column) so readings are interpreted correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between sensitivity and range / limits of improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Using lighter fluids can increase sensitivity 'but to such means of improvement there is a natural limit' (scale cannot be increased beyond certain ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When increasing sensitivity (e.g., lighter fluids), identify physical limits and practical side-effects; quantify how sensitivity scales with material choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability / multi-functionality of apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: By slight variation (closing both cisterns and applying trumpet mouths) the instrument 'may be made to serve the purpose of an Anemometer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design apparatus that can be adapted for related measurements with documented modifications; describe how small design changes yield new measurement capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of exposure/connection to test environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the horizontal pipe to a key‑hole or perforation transmits external pressure to the closed cistern and produces measurable changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure stable, reproducible coupling between instrument and tested environment (e.g., defined aperture connection) so that perturbations are produced and measured consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to confounding residual effects / baseline state (physiology)
rubrics_metrics.description: In digestion experiments: 'there is always some gastric juice ready to act on any new food... although the secretion of gastric juice ceases at the moment of the excision... some digested food must be found in the stomach for some hours after the operation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for pre-existing states or residual activity (e.g., residual gastric juice or partially digested food) that can mask or delay effects; design timing and baselines accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalization of feeding and handling across groups (control of animal appetite)
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge fairly 'the different animals must be allowed equally to satisfy their appetite, to eat till... the appetite has equally abated in all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control and/or match feeding and pre-experiment conditions across experimental and control subjects to avoid bias from differing hunger/consumption affecting outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of timing and survival interval in outcome assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Results depend on survival time: examinations at 5–6 hours differ from 18–20+ hours; 'the longer the animal lives after the excision... the less digested food is left.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose observation endpoints that capture the process under study; sample at multiple timepoints when processes evolve slowly or residual effects persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinded assessment / avoidance of observer bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Brodie was 'requested to examine and give his opinion ... without having been told which was which' and identified the healthy stomach by inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, use blinded outcome assessment so examiners are unaware of treatment assignment to reduce bias in qualitative judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appropriate mechanistic substitution controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Galvanism substituted for nervous power: 'the digestive process of the stomach supported by galvanism, is, as far as we can see, as perfect as that supported by the nervous power itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test mechanistic hypotheses by substituting candidate causal agents (e.g., electrical stimulation) and compare outcomes to infer mechanism, while acknowledging limits (only works in living tissue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of alternative explanations for positive results (critical interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical irritation experiments may be confounded by previously formed gastric juice or unequal feeding; 'In judging of the result of such experiments, several things must be taken into the account which appear to have escaped the attention of those gentlemen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly consider and rule out alternative explanations (residual secretions, feeding differences, procedural differences) before attributing causality to an intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication, public demonstration, and independent confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments were 'made publicly' and 'all who witnessed... admitted... none expressed a doubt respecting them' and several named observers corroborated results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public demonstration and independent witnessing/replication strengthen confidence in results; seek corroboration from other competent observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated factors affecting friction (Coulomb's five causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coulomb's list: 1) The nature of the bodies in contact. 2) The extent of surface. 3) The pressure on the surface. 4) The time the surfaces have been in contact. 5) The state of the atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying friction, explicitly consider and, where possible, vary/control these five factors and report their values and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of friction (time-dependent vs velocity-dependent; gliding vs rolling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coulomb distinguished friction generated 'by time' and friction 'by velocity'; others distinguish gliding and rolling friction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which type(s) of friction are relevant to the experiment and design measurements to separate static (time/equilibration) effects from velocity-dependent (dynamic) effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate static (initiation) and kinetic (maintenance) friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Results showed greater force often required to start motion than to keep it (examples: woods where maintaining motion required much less than initiating it; metals sometimes showed no difference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure both the force to initiate motion and the force to sustain motion; report both as they may differ substantially depending on materials and lubrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of surface preparation, polish, and cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Polishing diminishes asperities but may not change curvature; cohesion and surface conditioning (roughness) affect friction significantly (e.g., 'friction bears immediate reference to the elementary structure of bodies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report surface finish, treatments, and material cohesion; consider polishing, glazing, or wear history as key experimental parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale, velocity, and time‑to‑equilibrium considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some heterogeneous surface effects 'did not attain their limit sometimes for days'; velocities often had little influence except under special circumstances; scale (length/area) matters in large apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sufficient duration for systems to reach steady states; choose experimental scales and velocities representative of intended real-world conditions and report them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for complexity and contingencies in large machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Large machinery experiments showed anomalies (resistance varying with quantity of machinery, irregular movements, difficulties producing simultaneous actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complex systems, identify and control for emergent contingencies (synchronization, reversals, irregular motions); document elements that could not be controlled and their likely impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root experimental design in prior theory and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper reviews Amontons, Coulomb, Vince, and others, using prior experimental results to frame current investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground experimental hypotheses and variable selection in existing theoretical and empirical literature; compare and contrast with prior reported results.
